title: Velvet Analytics model roadmap and VPC playbook
summary: Initial technical discovery: Velvet Analytics is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Key concerns: context length up to 200k tokens for long docs, multilingual throughput (EN/ES/PT), tool-calling for data connectors, SOC2/KMS requirements, and pricing for a pilot. SE-led model tradeoffs discussed (quantized open models vs hosted proprietary), need for benchmark with their anonymized dataset. Next: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing, security pack, and test account for 2-week pilot.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs

transcript:
Header
Date: 2027-05-04 16:00 UTC
Duration: 47 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramos (Velvet CTO), Liam O'Neill (Platform Eng), Arjun Patel (ML Eng)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for making time today, quick check—can people hear me ok?
[00:03] Sofia Ramos: Yep, loud and clear. Sorry running a bit late had a standup overlap.
[00:06] Maya Chen: No worries. I'll do a short agenda: understand your model needs (context length, multilingual), how you plan to call tools/connectors, and then Ethan will do a quick technical walk through tradeoffs for hosted/dedicated/private.
[00:18] Liam O'Neill: Sounds good. We're primarily interested in using open models where possible but need to understand the ops and cost. Also long documents, like our research reports, can be 50–150k tokens, occasionally up to ~200k, so context window is critical.
[00:34] Ethan Ruiz: Got it, thanks. Quick clarification: when you say 150k tokens, is that single-turn context or you'd chunk and do RAG?
[00:42] Arjun Patel: It's a mix — sometimes single turn for summarization and timeline extraction we want as much context as possible, other times it's RAG where we call external db. We want tool-calling for connectors (internal DBs, Postgres, and an S3-like store).
[00:56] Maya Chen: Perfect. High level: Hosted API is fastest to get started, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput, and Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict data residency. For context windows there are two axes: model choice (some open models support longer context out of the box) and infra (you can chain or stitch contexts via KV cache or segmented attention).
[01:17] Sofia Ramos: Can you give examples of models you'd recommend for 100–200k? We looked at Mistral long-context variants and some Llama 3 forks.
[01:25] Ethan Ruiz: Sure. There are specialized long-context models (research and community forks) that can handle 64k–200k tokens, but throughput and latency hit. For 100k+ we typically recommend a hybrid: use a long-context encoder that ingests the document and produces dense vectors/KV cache, then smaller decoder for generation. Open models like Llama-family (2/3) can be quantized for Dedicated setups. Mistral 8x has good perf but durability for very long contexts is mixed. Also note proprietary models like Gemini aren't always available on Dedicated.
[01:58] Liam O'Neill: So is the plan to host the long-context encoder as a separate pipeline? That adds complexity — we'd prefer as few moving parts as possible.
[02:06] Ethan Ruiz: Yep, typically a preprocessor step — chunk+embed or streaming encoder — Redwood runtime supports KV caching and prefix caching so you can stitch requests; it's built-in for Dedicated and Private. In Hosted we can expose the same primitives but there are quota and cost tradeoffs.
[02:22] Arjun Patel: How about multilingual? We need EN/ES/PT and occasional FR and DE. Tokenization differences blow up token counts.
[02:29] Ethan Ruiz: Good point. Multilingual models vary. Some open models have full multilingual tokenizers and perform well; others do not. For Spanish/Portuguese you often see similar tokenization efficiency to English, but for languages with different scripts it changes. We recommend running a tokenization analysis — we can do that as part of the bench.
[02:45] Maya Chen: On the ops/security side, I know you mentioned SOC2 earlier — can you talk through mandatory controls?
[02:52] Sofia Ramos: Yes, SOC2 is required, plus SSO via SAML, RBAC, and KMS for key management. We also need audit logs that capture model version + request metadata for compliance.
[03:05] Maya Chen: Understood. Redwood Hosted is SOC2 compliant, we have SAML SSO and RBAC; we also offer customer-managed KMS in Dedicated and Private. Audit logs are part of the Console with per-route tracing. We'll send the SOC2 report and an integration doc.
[03:18] Liam O'Neill: For encryption keys, do you support HSM-backed keys?
[03:21] Ethan Ruiz: Yes, HSM/KMS integration is supported on Private; on Dedicated you can bring your own KMS. Hosted supports cloud KMS options but if you need an on-prem HSM that usually maps to Private deployment.
[03:31] Arjun Patel: About function/tool calling — we need to call internal connectors but also run code for data transforms. How does Redwood's tool-calling work in Dedicated?
[03:39] Ethan Ruiz: We support structured function calls in the API; in Dedicated/Private you can run your tool bridge inside your network, and the runtime supports safe serializations and policy controls. There is a patterns doc for secure tool-calling, rate limits, and fallbacks.
[03:52] Sofia Ramos: Any gotchas for RAG latency? If we have 200k doc ingestion and then cross-query, what latency numbers are realistic?
[03:59] Ethan Ruiz: For single request summarization over 100–200k it's typically higher latency — could be several seconds to tens of seconds depending on model size and batch. With Dedicated and optimized kernels + quantization, and prefix/KV caching, you can often get to lower tail latencies for repeated patterns. For RAG where you're retrieving passages, that is much faster because retrieval reduces the generation window.
[04:21] Maya Chen: Also cost — big context windows increase per-request compute. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and quantization profiles per workload to reduce unit costs; we'll propose quantized Llama 2- or 3- family for your pilot where quality is acceptable.
[04:33] Liam O'Neill: We care about reproducibility — model versioning and rollouts. Can Redwood pin versions and do canary rollouts?
[04:40] Ethan Ruiz: Yes, model pinning, canaries, A/B testing, and automatic fallback policies are part of Console. We'll link the rollout docs.
[04:49] Sofia Ramos: On data residency: most of our data must stay in EU. Is Redwood available in EU regions for Hosted?
[04:56] Maya Chen: Yes, Hosted has EU regions; Dedicated can be deployed in our EU cloud regions and Private obviously can be on-prem. We'll capture your region requirement in the pilot quote.
[05:06] Arjun Patel: For the benchmark, we want to include: 1) a worst-case single-turn 150–200k summarization, 2) a batch of 5k short multilingual queries, 3) tool-calling flow with Postgres connector.
[05:17] Ethan Ruiz: That's a good set. We'll need an anonymized sample of the long docs and a schema for the Postgres calls. I'll draft a benchmark plan.
[05:24] Maya Chen: Quick question Sofia — timeline and success criteria?
[05:27] Sofia Ramos: We're looking to pick a vendor within 6 weeks, pilot for 2–4 weeks, then production Q3. Success: 1) latency < 10s median for our main summarization path, 2) cost per 1k tokens within our target budget, and 3) security controls validated.
[05:44] Maya Chen: Good. Competitors — any we've already looked at?
[05:46] Sofia Ramos: We've trialed OpenAI for hosted and briefly evaluated Anthropic. OpenAI's LLMs were nice for quality but cost and data residency were concerns. Anthropic's tools were promising but integrations and pricing were a blocker.
[05:58] Ethan Ruiz: One nuance: when customers want both long context and tool-calling with low latency, Dedicated often hits the sweet spot — you get more control over kernels, model quantization, and KMS. Private if they need HSM or full air-gapped. Hosted for quick POC with smaller datasets.
[06:15] Liam O'Neill: Can Redwood spin up a Dedicated pilot for us? What's the minimum commitment?
[06:19] Maya Chen: We can do a short-term Dedicated pilot with a reduced commit for 30 days; pricing varies by GPU shape. I'll send options.
[06:25] Arjun Patel: On the ML side, we're worried about hallucinations when summarizing long reports. Any tooling to detect regressions?
[06:33] Ethan Ruiz: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets/evals. You can run continuous evals on production traffic and get alerts if metrics degrade.
[06:43] Sofia Ramos: Are there limitations on token-level metrics in Hosted? We need token-level billing per route for internal chargebacks.
[06:50] Maya Chen: Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and model. That's available across Hosted and Dedicated; in Private you can forward metrics back to your monitoring stack.
[06:59] Liam O'Neill: For model sizes, do you have recommendations for balancing cost vs quality? We're ok with some latency for better summaries but want to control monthly spend.
[07:08] Ethan Ruiz: Generally, medium-sized models (e.g., 13–33B) quantized are sweet spots for many summarization tasks; for highly nuanced reasoning or rare-domain knowledge, larger models help. We'll propose a few candidate models and cost profiles in the quote.
[07:21] Sofia Ramos: For multilingual accuracy we might opt for a multilingual fine-tuned model. Does Redwood support hosting customer fine-tunes?
[07:29] Maya Chen: We support serving user fine-tuned weights in Dedicated and Private. For Hosted, we have options for fine-tuning as a service but with some constraints. We'll include that in the pilot options.
[07:41] Arjun Patel: Slightly off-topic — latency percentiles. We need 95th < 15s ideally. Is that feasible with 100k context?
[07:49] Ethan Ruiz: For raw single-shot 100k context and large decoder, 95th will be higher unless you use advanced kernel optimizations and batching. With Dedicated + optimized kernels + empty concurrency tuning you can get closer. We'll benchmark to measure real numbers for your workload.
[08:03] (Brief crosstalk)
[08:06] Liam O'Neill: Ok, what does the benchmark deliverable look like?
[08:09] Ethan Ruiz: 1) test plan and scripts, 2) performance table (latency p50/p95, throughput), 3) cost estimate per 1M tokens, 4) qualitative evals for multilingual accuracy, and 5) notes on deployment config (batch sizes, kernel flags, quantization).
[08:27] Maya Chen: We'll also include a security appendix with SOC2, SSO, KMS, and audit logging details.
[08:33] Sofia Ramos: Great. On next steps, we'll share the sample docs and decide timing for the bench. Also send pilot pricing.
[08:40] Maya Chen: Noted. Any final quick questions?
[08:43] Arjun Patel: One more: outage/fallback strategies — if Dedicated region goes down, can Redwood route to Hosted or another region?
[08:50] Ethan Ruiz: Yes, smart routing supports fallback policies, you can route by region and cost tier and do automatic fallback to compatible model variants. We'll show you an example policy.
[08:59] Sofia Ramos: Perfect. Thanks.
[09:01] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs discussed and the benchmark plan.
[09:06] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-generated, occasional word substitution ("K-V cash" vs KV cache), timestamps approximate.
